title: Chapter 12: Recoding
text:
Quarto Set Up
In Chapter 11, you learned how to create a Quarto file, keep the YAML header, use Markdown headings, write memos outside code chunks, and control chunks with #| options. In this chapter, you will build two more Quarto skills that make your notes more readable and more reproducible:

add a table of contents and section numbering
use inline R code inside your sentences

🎯 Create a Quarto File

For those of you who have GitHub and a course project, navigate to your course folder and open your course project. This will open RStudio. Click “Pull” in the Git pane to get the latest version of the course materials. After completing work, save, stage, commit, and push.

If you don’t have GitHub or a course project, just open RStudio and set your working directory to your course folder.

Open a new Quarto document in your course folder and save it as: chapter12_notes.qmd (File > New File > Quarto Document).


toc: true
As your notes get longer, it becomes harder to scroll and find what you need. Quarto can automatically build a table of contents from your headings, and it can also number your sections for you. The main YAML options for this are toc: true, toc-depth:, and number-sections: true. These options are commonly placed in the document options near the top of the YAML.
Use this updated YAML header for Chapter 12:
---
title: "Chapter 12 Notes"
subtitle: "mutate() and case_when()"
author: "YOUR NAME"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
    number-sections: true
    embed-resources: true
---


What each part does:

title: gives your document a title.
subtitle: gives your document a subtitle.
author: puts your name on the document.
date: today inserts the current local date automatically. Quarto Dates and Date Formatting has more options for date formatting and dynamic date keywords.
format: tells Quarto what kind of output to create.
html: tells Quarto to render the document as an HTML file.
toc: true adds a table of contents automatically.
toc-depth: 2 tells Quarto to include level 1 and level 2 headings in the table of contents.
number-sections: true adds section numbers to your headings in the rendered document.
embed-resources: true keeps the HTML report self-contained so it is easier to submit and share.



Headings
You will want to use headings to see how the table of contents works. Create a simple outline for Chapter 12 using headings. Try using the following structure:

# Quarto Notes

# Load Packages

# Vectorized Conditionals

## ifelse()

## case_when()

## More than Two Categories

### Nested ifelse()

### Multiple Rule case_when()

# mutate()

## Column Copy

### mutate() with Arithmetic

### case_when() inside mutate()

## Overwrite Column Values
Render to HTML often to see the results. Render is like knit or preview.


Dynamic memoing
So far, you have used code chunks to run R code. Quarto also lets you place small pieces of R code directly inside normal sentences. This is called inline code. Inline code is useful when you want your written memo to automatically include a value computed by your R code. Quarto evaluates inline code during rendering, so the sentence stays up to date with your analysis.
In Quarto, inline code uses one pair of backticks and the engine name inside the backticks. For R, the pattern is:
`{r} expression`
🐱 This is a good place to be curious about how Quarto works. The code is written inside a sentence, but when the report renders, Quarto runs the code and shows the result. Very cool!

Inline Example
🎯 Imagine you want to write a sentence that says how many rows are in the filtered mtcars dataset. Instead of hardcoding the number, you can use inline code to compute it.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk
library(dplyr)
num_rows <- mtcars %>% 
  filter(cyl == 6) %>% 
  nrow()

Then, in your written memo, you can write the expression:
🗣 The filtered dataset has `{r} num_rows` rows.
When rendered to HTML, this will show as:
🗣 The filtered dataset has 7 rows.
In this chapter, use inline R code when you want your memo to report a computed value such as a vector length, category count, or converted measurement.

🎯 For this chapter, practice setting up your notes file so that:

the YAML includes a table of contents and section numbering
your headings organize the chapter clearly
your code chunks do the main work
your memos use inline R code whenever you want to report a value from your analysis

Now that you have created and saved your Quarto file, follow along with this guided practice and take notes. Fill in each section under the headings.
💡 Test render your document often to see how your notes are coming together. Do your inline code expressions show the expected values?



📦 Packages
In this chapter, you will use dplyr verbs and dslabs datasets.
Remember that you only need to install once install.packages("dplyr"); install.packages("dslabs").
🎯 Load the required packages at the beginning of your QMD.

library(dslabs)  # Data science labs package
library(dplyr)   # Data manipulation package

🐱 Messages and warnings are often clues. A curious analyst asks what R is trying to tell them before hiding the message. Check that your packages loaded correctly.

title: Chapter 12: Recoding
text:
Vectorized Conditional Functions
In previous chapters, you used logical conditions to keep some values and drop others, or to replace selected values in place. In this chapter, you will use logical conditions in a third way: to return a result for every element. That is what functions like ifelse() and case_when() do.
Logical conditions in R can do more than select values. They can also be used to return a new vector by assigning an output to each element based on one or more rules. Functions such as ifelse() and case_when() are called vectorized conditional functions because they evaluate conditions element-by-element across a vector and return a new vector of the same length.
This section builds on ideas you already know. In earlier chapters, you used conditions to keep values or rows with logical subsetting, and to replace selected values with subassignment. Now you will use conditions in a new way: not to drop or replace selected cases, but to return a result for every position. Those results are often used inside mutate() to create or modify columns.
Subsetting keeps some values and drops others. Vectorized conditionals, by contrast, keep all positions and assign each one a result. In other words, subsetting answers “What do I keep?” while vectorized conditionals answer “What value should I return for each element?”

Review Subsetting with Conditions
Subsetting answers the question, “Which values or rows do I keep?” With a vector, logical indexing uses a pattern of TRUE and FALSE values to keep or modify selected positions.

# 📖 Review
## Create vector x
x <- 1:6
## logical vector
x > 3

[1] FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE



# 📖 Review
## logical subsetting
x[x > 3]

[1] 4 5 6


🗣 x[x > 3] subsets x to keep only values greater than 3. The expression x > 3 creates a logical vector of TRUE and FALSE values.
🧐 Notice: You used the same idea with data frames in Chapter 11. The filter() function also applies a logical condition, but at the row level, keeping rows that satisfy the condition and dropping the rest.


Review Subassignment
Subsetting is used to replace values, called subassignment. When you assign a value to a subset of an object, you are replacing the values in those positions.

# 📖 Review
## replaces values
x[x > 3] <- 99
## ✅  print result
x

[1]  1  2  3 99 99 99


🗣 x[x > 3] subsets x to keep only the values greater than 3, and x[x > 3] <- 99 uses logical indexing to replace those matching values with 99.

This review example uses a condition to identify matching cases. The difference is what happens next:

Subsetting keeps only matching values or rows.
Subassignment changes only matching values.
Vectorized conditionals return a result for every position.

That is the key new idea in this section. Vectorized conditional functions such as ifelse() and case_when() still test conditions element-by-element, but they do not drop nonmatching cases. Instead, they evaluate a condition for each element and return a new vector with one result for every position.
When this new vector is used inside mutate(), a function shown at the end of this chapter, it becomes a new column rather than a subset of the old one.


Simple ifelse()
Base R describes ifelse() as returning a value with the same shape as the test, filled from yes or no.
📜 The SYNTAX: ifelse(test, yes, no)

test – logical vector (TRUE/FALSE/NA)
yes – value to insert where test is TRUE
no – value to insert where test is FALSE.
NA – if NA, the result is NA at that position.

🎯 Label the vector of numbers greater than 3 as “Large” and others as “Small”.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk: 
x <- c(3, 2, 3, 6, 5)


# ✅  Pre-check
length(x)

[1] 5



🐱 Inline R is worth practicing because it does something unusual: it lets code work inside paragrgaph sentences. I want to see whether Quarto can ask R for the length of x and place the answer directly in my memo.
🗣 `x` is a vector with 5 values.
When rendered to HTML, this should read:
🗣 x is a vector with 5 values.
💡 Test render. Does the sentence show the expected number of values in x? If not, check your code and try again. ___

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk: 
ifelse(test = x > 3, yes = "Large", no = "Small")

[1] "Small" "Small" "Small" "Large" "Large"


🗣 The output positions for 3 and under are “Small” and numbers higher than 3 are “Large”.

# ✅  Verify
length(ifelse(x > 3, "Large", "Small"))

[1] 5


🗣 The result has the same length as x. Nothing was dropped. Each position got a label.
🐱 This is the curiosity move here: I am checking whether ifelse() gave one answer back for each value I started with. I might wonder about the pattern of "Large" and "Small" later, but first I need to understand what this function returns.

🧐 Notice: Arguments, such as test, yes, and no in ifelse(), are often not required to be named inside of functions.

💡 Tip: Read this ifelse() statement like ‘If the vector is greater than 3, then return “Large”, otherwise return “Small”.’

📖 x[x > 3] logical subsetting keeps only matches
📖 x[x > 3] <- 99 subassignment replaces only matches
⚡ ifelse(x > 3, "Large", "Small") returns a new vector with a value for every position based on the condition.



Simple case_when()
dplyr describes case_when() as a general vectorized if-else that evaluates rules in order and uses the first match for each element. This makes it especially useful when you have several categories to assign.
dplyr::case_when() can do exactly what ifelse() is doing.
📜 The SYNTAX: case_when(condition1 ~ value1, condition2 ~ value2, .default = default_value)
The ~ symbol means “maps to” or “yields”.
The .default argument specifies the value to return when no conditions are TRUE. If you omit .default and no conditions match, case_when() will return NA for those positions.
🎯 Label the vector of numbers greater than 3 as “Large” and others as “Small”.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk: 
case_when(c(3, 2, 3, 6, 5) > 3 ~ "Large", .default = "Small")

[1] "Small" "Small" "Small" "Large" "Large"


🗣 The output positions for 3 and under are “Small” and numbers higher than 3 are “Large”.

⚡ case_when(c(3, 2, 3, 6, 5) > 3 ~ "Large", .default = "Small") returns a new vector with a value for every position based on the condition.


📖 Why do we need both ifelse() and case_when()? case_when() is usually clearer once you have 3+ categories.


More Than Two Categories
ifelse() is designed for two categories. If you have more than two, you can nest ifelse() statements inside each other, but this quickly becomes hard to read. case_when() is designed for multiple categories and is much easier to read when you have more than two conditions.

# ✅  Setup
# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk: 
scores <- c(55, 65, 75, 85, 95)

🎯 Re-code scores less than 60 as “Low”, scores less than 80 as “Medium”, and all others as “High”.

Nested ifelse()
🎯 Re-code scores less than 60 as “Low”, scores less than 80 as “Medium”, and all others as “High” using nested ifelse().

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk: 
ifelse(scores < 60, "Low",
       ifelse(scores < 80, "Medium", "High"))

[1] "Low"    "Medium" "Medium" "High"   "High"  


🗣 This works, but the logic is nested inside the no argument of the first ifelse(), which becomes harder to read as the number of categories grows.


Multiple Rule case_when()
case_when() avoids the ugly nesting that happens with repeated ifelse() calls. It is a general vectorized if-else: R checks the rules from top to bottom and uses the first rule that matches each element. That is why the order of the rules matters.
🎯 Code scores less than 60 as "Low", scores less than 80 as "Medium", and all others as "High" using case_when().

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
case_when(scores < 60 ~ "Low",
          scores < 80 ~ "Medium",
          TRUE        ~ "High")

[1] "Low"    "Medium" "Medium" "High"   "High"  


🗣 This reads more like a set of classification rules: first check for "Low", then check for "Medium", and assign "High" to everything else.
⚠️ The order of the rules matters because case_when() uses the first condition that matches.
🐱 This is a good place to be curious and test what happens when the rules are in the wrong order. The goal is not to break the code randomly; the goal is to see how case_when() makes its decision.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
case_when(
  scores < 80 ~ "Medium",
  scores < 60 ~ "Low",
  TRUE       ~ "High"
)

[1] "Medium" "Medium" "Medium" "High"   "High"  


🗣 This does not work as intended. Any score less than 60 also satisfies scores < 80, so those values are labeled "Medium" before R ever checks the "Low" rule.
💡 Tip: write rules from most specific to more general, and end with a default rule such as TRUE ~ "High".

So far, ifelse() and case_when() have returned new vectors. That is useful, but most data work happens inside data frames. Next, you will use mutate() to store those new values as columns.

title: Chapter 12: Recoding
text:
mutate()
So far, case_when() has returned a new vector of labels. In real data analysis, you usually want to store that result in a data frame as a new column. That is what mutate() does.
mutate() creates new columns that are functions of existing columns. It can also modify an existing column if you reuse the same column name.
📜 The SYNTAX:
mutate(data, new_col = expression)
Or with piping
name_data <- data %>% mutate(new_col = expression)

data is the data frame you are working with.
new_col is the name of the new column you want to create.
expression is the vector or calculation you want to store in that column.

You can think of mutate() as saying: “Take this data frame, and add a new column based on these existing columns.”
📖 The key idea is this:

A new name on the left side of = adds a new column.
An existing name on the left side of = overwrites that column.
The right side of = tells R what values to put there.


Column Copy
🎯 Create a new column that is a copy of am in mtcars.

# ✅  Pre-Check
names(mtcars) # Check the column names

 [1] "mpg"  "cyl"  "disp" "hp"   "drat" "wt"   "qsec" "vs"   "am"   "gear"
[11] "carb"



# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars2 <- mtcars %>% 
  mutate(new_column_copy = am)

🗣 In a new data set called mtcars2, a new column named new_column_copy is created that is identical to the am column.

# ✅ Verify
names(mtcars2) # Check the column names again

 [1] "mpg"             "cyl"             "disp"            "hp"             
 [5] "drat"            "wt"              "qsec"            "vs"             
 [9] "am"              "gear"            "carb"            "new_column_copy"


This simple example shows that mutate() can create a new column from an existing one. The right side of mutate() is for calculations or rule-based expressions on existing columns. We’ll start by using calculations inside mutate() to create a new column.

mutate() with Arithmetic
Doing unit conversions is a common data analyst task. Here it is in action.

# ✅  Setup
measurements <- data.frame(height_in = c(60, 65, 70))
measurements

  height_in
1        60
2        65
3        70



🐱 This is a small but useful thing to wonder about: can Quarto pull a column name directly from R into a sentence? Let’s try it before we add a new column.
🗣 The `measurements` data frame has one column: height\_in.
When rendered to HTML, this should read:
🗣 The measurements data frame has one column: height_in

🎯 Create a new column called height_cm that converts inches to centimeters (1 inch = 2.54 cm).

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
measurements %>%
  mutate(height_cm = height_in * 2.54)

  height_in height_cm
1        60     152.4
2        65     165.1
3        70     177.8


🗣 mutate(height_cm = height_in * 2.54) creates a new column called height_cm. Each value in height_cm is calculated from the matching value in height_in.


case_when() inside mutate()
The right side of mutate() can also be a rule-based expression. One common example is case_when() which lets you build a new categorical variable from an existing numeric variable.

# ✅  Setup
student_scores <- data.frame(scores = c(55, 68, 72, 83, 91))

🎯 Create a new column called score_level that labels each score from scores as "Low", "Medium", or "High".

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
student_scores <- student_scores %>%
  mutate(
    score_level = case_when(
      scores < 60 ~ "Low",
      scores < 80 ~ "Medium",
      TRUE        ~ "High"
    )
  )

🗣 mutate() adds a new column called score_level. The values in that column come from the rules inside case_when().

student_scores is the data frame.
mutate(...) adds a new column.
score_level = names that new column.
case_when(...) decides what label to return for each row based on the value in scores.


# ✅ Verify
head(student_scores)

  scores score_level
1     55         Low
2     68      Medium
3     72      Medium
4     83        High
5     91        High



🐱 Now I want to practice using inline R to report the current column names in my memo.
🗣 `student_scores` has the columns scores and score\_level.
When rendered to HTML, this should read:
🗣 student_scores has the columns scores and score_level.
💡 Test render.
🐱 Looking at this code, I might wonder how paste() works. Rather than guessing, I could check ?paste in RStudio’s Help pane. names(student_scores) gets the column names, and paste(..., collapse = " and ") combines them into a single piece of text separated by the word “and”. Notice the space before and after the and between the quotes `” and “. Those spaces are included in the output, so the column names appear with space around the word”add”.
🛠 Break Things!
Test render without the spaces to see the difference:
🗣 `student_scores` has the columns scoresandscore\_level.
💡 Test render.

The mutate() + case_when() duo is a powerful way to create new variables based on complex rules. You can have as many conditions as you need, and you can use existing columns in your data frame to build those rules.
In some situations, you may want to overwrite an existing column instead of creating a new one. That is also possible with mutate(), as the next section shows.



Overwrite Column Values
mutate() will overwrite an existing column when you reuse the same column name on the left side of =. We’ll use case_when() to recode the values in the am column of mtcars from numeric to categorical labels.
🐱 Overwriting is a place to slow down and be curious before running the code. I want to know what the original values are first, because after overwriting, those original 0 and 1 values will no longer be in the new data frame.
🎯 Recode the am column in mtcars from 0/1 to “Automatic”/“Manual”.

# ✅  Pre-check
unique(mtcars$am) 

[1] 1 0


🗣 am is a numeric column with two unique values: 0 and 1.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
cars_overwrite <- mtcars %>%
  mutate(
    am = case_when(
      am == 0 ~ "Automatic", 
      TRUE ~ "Manual")
    )


# ✅ Verify:
unique(cars_overwrite$am)

[1] "Manual"    "Automatic"



🐱 Practice inline R code to dynamically report within a memo:
🗣 The `am` column in `cars_overwrite` has the unique values: Manual, Automatic.
When rendered to HTML, this should read:
🗣 The am column in cars_overwrite has the unique values: Manual, Automatic.
🗣 The am column has been changed from 0/1 to "Automatic"/"Manual".
💡 Test render. ___
📖 Overwrite Key Takeaway
In every example above, mutate() followed the same pattern:

the left side of = named the output column
the right side of = created its values

When the left side is a new name, R adds a new column. When the left side reused an existing name, R overwrites that column.

title: Chapter 12: Recoding
text:
Summary
In this chapter, you learned that logical conditions in R can do more than keep or replace values: they can also return a new result for every element. You practiced this with ifelse() for simple two-way decisions and case_when() for multi-rule classification, then used mutate() to store those results as new or overwritten columns in a data frame. You also continued building your Quarto workflow by adding a table of contents, section numbering, and inline R code so your notes can report values dynamically and stay reproducible.
You also practiced curiosity as a learning habit. The 🐱 notes modeled how to pause, wonder how a tool works, test what R returns, and check whether the result matches what you expected. Curiosity in this chapter is not random exploring. It means asking a useful question, checking the evidence, and knowing when to keep going with the main task.

title: Chapter 12: Recoding
text:
Chapter Terms
Arguments: Inputs that you provide to functions to customize their behavior. Arguments are specified within the parentheses of a function call and can modify how the function operates or what data it processes.
case_when(): A dplyr function used to apply multiple conditional rules across a vector. case_when() checks conditions in order and returns the value connected to the first condition that is TRUE, making it useful for recoding values or creating categories from several rules.
Curiosity: A learning habit that means noticing something worth understanding, asking a useful question, checking what R returns, and deciding whether to investigate further or stay focused on the current task. Curiosity drives your intrinsic motivation to learn, ask questions, and seek understanding.
ifelse(): A base R function that applies a simple conditional rule across a vector. ifelse() checks each element of a logical test and returns one value when the test is TRUE and another value when the test is FALSE.
Logical Indexing: Indexing a vector using a logical vector of TRUE/FALSE values (for example, x[x > 0]) so R keeps the elements where the index is TRUE and drops those where it is FALSE. If the logical index is a different length, R may recycle it, which can lead to surprising results.
Logical Vector: A vector that stores Boolean elements: TRUE or FALSE (and sometimes NA for missing). Logical vectors are commonly produced by comparisons (for example, x > 0) and are heavily used for filtering and conditional code.
mutate(): A dplyr function used to create, change, or remove columns in a data frame or tibble. mutate() is commonly used to add new variables based on existing variables while keeping the same rows
Overwrite: A common type of subassignment where you change existing values (you replace what is already there).
Subsetting: Selecting a smaller piece of an R object using indices (positions, names, or a logical mask). With data frames, subsetting most commonly uses [ in the form df[rows, cols] and typically preserves the object’s structure (e.g., you still get a data frame when you subset rows and columns).
Subassignment: Replacing part of an object by putting an index on the left side of <-. R changes only the indexed part of the object. Examples: x[i] <- value, df[rows, "col"] <- value, df[[col]] <- value, df$col <- value.
Vectorized conditional: A function or expression that evaluates a condition element-by-element across a vector and returns an output for every element, producing a new vector of the same length. Unlike subsetting, which keeps some values and drops others, vectorized conditionals such as ifelse() and case_when() keep all positions and assign each one a result based on the condition.

text:
📝 Practice Space
In this Practice Space, you will use vectorized conditional functions to create clearer variables. Open-mindedness means comparing reasonable methods and choosing the approach that makes the code easiest to read, check, and explain. title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
Overview
In Chapters 11 and 12, you learned how to subset and transform data with dplyr using functions such as select(), filter(), mutate(), and case_when(). In this chapter, you will extend that workflow by learning how to organize data into groups and then calculate summaries for those groups. You will use count() to make frequency tables, summarize() to compute statistics such as mean and standard deviation, and group_by() to tell R which subgroups to analyze separately. You will also practice computing multiple statistics at once and working with more than one grouping variable.
This chapter is about learning when and how to ask R for grouped summaries, and then explaining what those summaries mean. You will also practice curiosity as a learning skill. Curiosity helps you pause before running code, predict what the output might show, check whether the result matches your question, and decide when a side question is worth exploring or when it is better to stay focused on the chapter goal.
At the same time, you will continue building reproducible workflow habits in Quarto by using headings, rendering often, checking your output, and memoing what your code is doing and what you learned from it.
By the end of Chapter 13 you will be able to:
Keep these goals in mind as you move through each section.

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
📖 Counts, Center, and Spread
Before using summarize() and count(), it helps to review a few data words you have likely seen before. You do not need to calculate these by hand in this chapter. You do need to understand what they mean so you can choose the right function and explain your results.
🐱 Curiosity as an intellectual virtue means choosing where to spend your attention. If these review terms feel rusty, pause here and use this section to refresh them. If you already practiced these ideas (e.g., in the Data Understanding Notebook activity), you can skip this review section and jump to dplyr’s count(). Return if you need a reminder.

Data Terminology
A numeric variable stores numbers that can be measured or calculated, such as mpg, height, or test score.
A categorical variable stores labels or group names, such as state, disease, or cylinder count.
In this chapter, we often group by a categorical variable and then summarize a numeric variable.


Count
A count tells you how many observations there are.

For a whole dataset, count means the total number of rows.
For grouped data, count means the number of rows in each group.

If you want to know how many cars have 4 cylinders, 6 cylinders, or 8 cylinders, you are asking for a count.


Center
Center describes a typical value.

Mean
The mean is the average.
It adds the values and divides by how many values there are.
If the mean mpg for cars with 4 cylinders is higher than the mean mpg for cars with 8 cylinders, then the 4-cylinder cars are more fuel efficient on average.


Median
The median is the middle value when the data are sorted.
🪞 Median is useful when extreme values might pull the mean too high or too low.



Spread
Spread describes how much the values vary.

Standard Deviation
The standard deviation tells you how far values tend to be from the mean.

A small standard deviation means the values are packed closely together.
A large standard deviation means the values are more spread out.

If one cylinder group has a much larger standard deviation for mpg, that group has more variability in fuel efficiency.


Range
The range is the distance from the smallest value to the largest value.
🪞 Range gives a quick sense of spread, but it only uses the minimum and maximum values.

🐱 The goal is to know which summary tool matches the question.

use count when you want to know how many rows are in a dataset or group
use mean when you want an average
use standard deviation when you want to describe spread
use a categorical variable to make groups
use a numeric variable when calculating statistics like mean or standard deviation

We’ll start with counting categories with count() because counts help you see what categories are present before you calculate more complex summaries.

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
dplyr’s count()
You can use count() to quickly count rows for each category or combination of categories.
count() is especially useful when you want a frequency table.
?count
📜 The SYNTAX
data %>% count(variable_name)
Or, for more than one grouping variable:
data %>% count(variable1, variable2, ...)

Count one variable
🎯 Count how many cars have each cylinder value.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars %>%
  count(cyl)

  cyl  n
1   4 11
2   6  7
3   8 14


🗣 The code above counts how many rows fall into each value of cyl. The result is a new table with one row per cylinder value and a column named n that stores the counts.
🐱 This is the curiosity move here: before I compare or explain anything, I want to know what categories are in the data and how many rows belong to each one. This step helps me understand the data before I ask a bigger data question.
💡 Test knit. Does the table show one row for each cylinder value and a column named n?

count() versus length()
length() counts how many values are in a vector.
count() counts rows in a data frame for each category or combination of categories.


count() with sorting
Sometimes you want to see the biggest groups first.
🎯 Count cars by cylinder and sort from largest count to smallest count.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars %>%
  count(cyl, sort = TRUE)

  cyl  n
1   8 14
2   4 11
3   6  7


🗣 sort = TRUE arranges the result so the largest count appears first. The counts are the same as before; only the row order changed.



Count multiple variables
You can also count combinations of categories.
🐱 This is a good time to indulge curiosity a little further. Counting one variable told us how many cars had each cylinder value. Counting two variables lets us ask a more specific question: how are cylinder values distributed across transmission types?
🎯 Count how many cars fall into each combination of cylinder count and transmission type.

🧐 Notice: In mtcars, am is a coded transmission variable. A value of 0 means automatic, and a value of 1 means manual.


# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars %>%
  count(cyl, am)

  cyl am  n
1   4  0  3
2   4  1  8
3   6  0  4
4   6  1  3
5   8  0 12
6   8  1  2


🗣 count(cyl, am) creates one row for each unique combination of cyl and am, then counts how many rows are in each combination.

This is useful when one grouping variable is not enough.
If our question is only “How many rows are in each category?”, count() is enough. But what if our question asks about averages, maximums, spread, or other statistics? We’ll need summarize().

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
dplyr’s summarize()
You can use summarize() to compute summary statistics like the mean, median, etc.
?summarize
📜 The SYNTAX
data %>% summarize(new_column_name = some_operation(column_name))
🎯 Find the overall mean mpg for all cars.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars %>% 
  summarize(mean_mpg = mean(mpg))

  mean_mpg
1 20.09062


🗣 The code above creates a new column called mean_mpg that contains the mean of the mpg column from the mtcars dataset.
We name the new column using new_name = calculation.
🎯 Find several summary statistics for mpg: mean, max, and count of cars.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars %>% 
  summarize(mean_mpg = mean(mpg),
            max_mpg = max(mpg),
            count = n())

  mean_mpg max_mpg count
1 20.09062    33.9    32



🧐 Notice: Do not put pipes %>% inside summarize(). Inside the function, separate each summary calculation with a comma ,.

💡 Test knit. Does the output show one row with three summary columns: mean_mpg, max_mpg, and count?

🤔 summary() is a base R function that gives a quick overall description of an object, such as basic statistics for each variable in a data frame. summarize() from dplyr is used to create your own summary results, usually after group_by(), such as the mean or count for each group.

count() versus summarize()
You can often get the same result in two ways.
🎯 Use group_by() and summarize() to produce the same counts by cylinder.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarize(n = n())

# A tibble: 3 × 2
    cyl     n
  <dbl> <int>
1     4    11
2     6     7
3     8    14


🗣 This gives the same idea as count(cyl). The difference is that count() is shorter and faster to write when your main goal is just to count rows.
Use count() when you mainly want frequencies. Use group_by() with summarize() when you want to calculate other statistics too, such as mean and standard deviation.

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
dplyr’s group_by()
group_by() changes the behavior of summary functions.
📜 The SYNTAX
data %>% group_by(variable1, variable2, ...) %>% some_operation()
🎯 Find the mean mpg for each cylinder count.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
cyl_means <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarize(mean_mpg = mean(mpg))

🗣 group_by(cyl) splits the cars into groups based on cylinder count, and summarize() calculates mean(mpg) for each group. mean_mpg is the name of the new summary column.

🧐 Notice: We chain group_by() and summarize() together using the pipe operator %>%. First, group_by(cyl) tells R to work separately by cylinder value. Then, summarize() calculates the mean mpg for each group.


# ✅ 
cyl_means  

# A tibble: 3 × 2
    cyl mean_mpg
  <dbl>    <dbl>
1     4     26.7
2     6     19.7
3     8     15.1


🐱 This is the main curiosity move in Chapter 13. We are no longer asking, “What is the overall mean?” We’re asking, “Does the mean change across groups?” Grouping helps us ask a sharper question without leaving the learning goal.
💡 Test knit. Does cyl_means print as a small table with one row per cylinder value?
🤔 Grouping cars by cyl is useful because cars with different numbers of cylinders often have different fuel efficiency, so one overall average mpg would hide those differences. By grouping first, you can compare the typical mpg for 4-, 6-, and 8-cylinder cars separately.

Explicit vs. Default Naming
If you do not give the summary column a name, dplyr uses the summary expression itself as the column name by default. So summarize(mean(mpg)) creates a column named mean(mpg) instead of a cleaner name like mean_mpg.
🎯 Find the mean mpg for each cylinder count without naming the summary column.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarize(mean(mpg))      

# A tibble: 3 × 2
    cyl `mean(mpg)`
  <dbl>       <dbl>
1     4        26.7
2     6        19.7
3     8        15.1


🗣 The default column name is the code itself: mean(mpg). Default names can be confusing when reading or sharing results, so naming summary columns makes tables clearer.
🐱 Notice the problem and build the habit of naming summary columns clearly.

Now that you have seen how group_by() changes one summary calculation, you can ask for several summary statistics at the same time.

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
Multiple Statistics
🎯 Create several summary columns in one summarize() call, separated by commas.
🐱 This is useful curiosity: one statistic rarely tells the whole story. A mean tells me the center, a standard deviation tells me about spread, and n() tells me how many rows were used for each group.
Use ?n to learn about the n() function.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
cyl_stats <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarize(mean_mpg = mean(mpg),
            sd_mpg   = sd(mpg),
            n        = n())


# ✅ Verify
cyl_stats

# A tibble: 3 × 4
    cyl mean_mpg sd_mpg     n
  <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <int>
1     4     26.7   4.51    11
2     6     19.7   1.45     7
3     8     15.1   2.56    14


🗣 n() counts how many rows are in each group created by group_by().
🤔 It is similar to count() because both tell you how many observations are in a group, but n() is used inside summarize() when you are also calculating other statistics.

🧐 Notice: length() counts the number of elements in an object. For a vector, that means the number of values. For a data frame, length() counts columns, not rows. That is why n() is the clearer tool here.

💡 Test knit. Does the output show one row for each cylinder value and three summary columns: mean_mpg, sd_mpg, and n?

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
Multiple Variables
group_by() with one column creates one group for each unique value in that column. group_by() with two columns creates one group for each unique combination of values.
🐱 This is a good moment to make a prediction before running the code. Curiosity is pausing long enough to make a reasonable guess, then checking that guess against the output.
❓ How many groups will group_by(cyl, am) create?
🎯 Predict how many groups will be created by group_by(cyl, am) before running the code.

# ✅ Pre-check
# Recall that mtcars$cyl has three unique values:
sort(unique(mtcars$cyl))

[1] 4 6 8

# Recall that mtcars$am has two unique values:
sort(unique(mtcars$am))

[1] 0 1


🗣 Two variables with 3 and 2 unique values can create \(3 \times 2 = 6\) possible groups.
🎯 Find the mean mpg for each combination of cylinder count and transmission type.

🧐 Notice: In mtcars, am is a coded transmission variable. A value of 0 means automatic, and a value of 1 means manual.


# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl, am) %>%
  summarize(avg_mpg = mean(mpg),
            count = n())

# A tibble: 6 × 4
# Groups:   cyl [3]
    cyl    am avg_mpg count
  <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
1     4     0    22.9     3
2     4     1    28.1     8
3     6     0    19.1     4
4     6     1    20.6     3
5     8     0    15.0    12
6     8     1    15.4     2


🗣:

Group 1: cyl = 4, am = 0 (4-cylinder automatic cars)
Group 2: cyl = 4, am = 1 (4-cylinder manual cars)
Group 3: cyl = 6, am = 0 (6-cylinder automatic cars)
Group 4: cyl = 6, am = 1 (6-cylinder manual cars)
Group 5: cyl = 8, am = 0 (8-cylinder automatic cars)
Group 6: cyl = 8, am = 1 (8-cylinder manual cars)

💡 Test knit. Does the output show one row for each cyl and am combination?

If you see a message about grouped output, keep going. The next section explains what that message means.

ungroup()
When you summarize data that has more than one grouping variable, dplyr may keep part of the grouping structure in the result. That leftover grouping can affect later code, so it is important to check whether your summary table is still grouped.
🐱 We are asking, “What did R keep behind the scenes, and could that affect my next step?”

A. Default behavior: keeps earlier groups
🎯 Show that with two grouping variables, summarize() keeps the earlier group by default.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
# A) Default behavior: "drop_last" (keeps earlier groups)
cyl_gear_stats <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl, gear) %>%
  summarize(mean_mpg = mean(mpg))   # no .groups set

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by cyl and gear.
ℹ Output is grouped by cyl.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(cyl, gear))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.



# ✅  Verify
group_vars(cyl_gear_stats)  # what groups remain?

[1] "cyl"



# ✅ Verify
is_grouped_df(cyl_gear_stats) # expect TRUE

[1] TRUE


🗣 The default behavior is .groups = "drop_last". That means summarize() drops the last grouping variable, gear, but keeps the earlier grouping variable, cyl.
You’ll want to be explicit when you do not want any grouping left.


B. Make it explicit inside summarize()
🎯 Return a plain, ungrouped table by telling summarize() to drop all groups.

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
# B) Make it explicit: drop *all* groups in the result
cyl_gear_stats_drop <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl, gear) %>%
  summarize(mean_mpg = mean(mpg), .groups = "drop")

🗣 The .groups argument starts with a period and "drop" must be written in quotation marks.

# ✅ Verify
group_vars(cyl_gear_stats_drop)  # expect character(0)

character(0)



# ✅ Verify
is_grouped_df(cyl_gear_stats_drop) # expect FALSE

[1] FALSE


🗣 Using .groups = "drop" tells summarize() to remove all grouping after the summary operation, resulting in a plain data frame without any grouping structure.
💡 Test knit. Does group_vars(cyl_gear_stats_drop) return character(0) and does is_grouped_df(cyl_gear_stats_drop) return FALSE?


C. Alternative: drop groups after summarizing
🎯 Achieve the same ungrouped result by using ungroup() after summarize()

# ⚡ Type this in a Quarto code chunk:
# C) Alternative: drop groups after summarizing
cyl_gear_stats_ungroup <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl, gear) %>%
  summarize(mean_mpg = mean(mpg)) %>%
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by cyl and gear.
ℹ Output is grouped by cyl.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(cyl, gear))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.



# ✅  Verify
group_vars(cyl_gear_stats_ungroup)  # expect character(0)

character(0)



# ✅ Verify
is_grouped_df(cyl_gear_stats_ungroup) # expect FALSE

[1] FALSE


🗣 Using ungroup() after summarize() removes all grouping from the resulting data frame. This gives the same ungrouped result as using .groups = "drop" inside summarize().
🐱 When we are done summarizing by groups, we want remove grouping for a plain table.
Pick one method and use it consistently: - Use .groups = "drop" when you want to remove grouping inside summarize(). - Use ungroup() when you want to remove grouping as a separate step after summarizing.

Speaking of summarizing, we’ve made it to the end of the chapter. Let’s review what you learned.

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
Summary
In this chapter, you learned how to describe data by groups using dplyr. You reviewed the basic ideas of count, center, and spread so you could interpret grouped results, then used count() to make frequency tables, summarize() to compute statistics, and group_by() to split a dataset into subgroups before summarizing. You also practiced calculating multiple statistics in one call, using n() inside summarize() to count rows within groups, and working with combinations of grouping variables.
Most importantly, you learned that grouping changes what a summary means. Instead of one result for the whole dataset, you can produce separate results for each category or combination of categories. This is a core skill for later data analysis because analysts often need to compare subgroups, not just describe an entire dataset with one number.
🐱 You also practiced curiosity as part of your workflow. In this chapter, curiosity meant pausing to ask what a summary is actually showing, predicting how many groups R might create, checking whether the output matched your expectation, and deciding when to investigate further versus when to stay focused on the current learning goal.


Table 1. Functions for grouped summaries







Function
Purpose




count()
Counts how many rows fall into each value or combination of values. Useful for frequency tables.


group_by()
Creates groups based on one or more variables so later summary functions work separately for each group.


summarize()
Creates a smaller summary table by calculating one or more summary statistics.


n()
Counts the number of rows in the current group when used inside summarize().


mean()
Calculates the average of numeric values.


sd()
Calculates the standard deviation, which describes spread around the mean.


max()
Finds the largest value in a vector.


unique()
Shows the distinct values in a vector. Useful for checking possible groups before summarizing.


length()
Counts the number of elements in an object. For a vector, it counts values. For a data frame, it counts columns, not rows.


.groups = "drop"
Removes grouping inside summarize() so the result is returned as an ungrouped table.


ungroup()
Removes grouping after a grouped operation has already been created.

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
Chapter Terms
Categorical Data: Data whose values place observations into groups or categories. The categories may have no natural order (nominal) or may have an order with uneven gaps between categories (ordinal). In R, categorical data are often stored as factors.
Center: The middle or typical location of a dataset. Measures of center, such as the mean and median, summarize where values tend to cluster.
Count: The number of observations or values in a dataset, group, or category. In introductory statistics, count tells you how many cases are present.
Frequency: The number of times a value or category appears in a dataset.
Mean: The arithmetic average of a set of numbers, found by adding all values and dividing by the number of values.
Median: The middle value in an ordered dataset. If there is an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values.
Numerical Data: Data recorded as numbers, where the values have meaningful magnitudes and consistent intervals. Numerical data are also called quantitative data.
Pipe: An operator that passes the result of one step directly into the next step, letting you write code as a readable sequence of actions instead of nesting functions inside each other. In tidyverse code, the pipe is usually %>%, so x %>% f() means “take x, then apply f()”; in newer base R, a similar built-in pipe is |>.
Range: A simple measure of spread found by subtracting the smallest value from the largest value in a dataset.
Spread: How much the values in a dataset vary or scatter rather than cluster tightly together. Common measures of spread include range, interquartile range (IQR), variance, and standard deviation.
Standard Deviation: A measure of spread that describes how far values typically vary from the mean. A small standard deviation means values are clustered close to the mean, while a large standard deviation means they are more spread out.

title: Chapter 13: Grouped Summaries
text:
📝 Practice Space
In this Practice Space, you will use grouped summaries to describe data in a reproducible report. You will practice count() for frequency tables, group_by() for creating groups, summarize() for calculating statistics, and n() for counting rows inside grouped summaries. chapter13_practice.qmd

Open-mindedness means comparing reasonable methods and choosing the approach that makes the code easiest to read, check, and explain. If you encounter an error, document your tenacity by briefly noting what happened, what you tried, and how you fixed it or what still confuses you. Document how you troubleshot the error and what resource(s) you used to help you resolve the issue (transparency). Show courage by sharing your thinking process, even if it includes mistakes, confusion, or a question you are still working through. Task 1
🌟 Single grouping
Using the stars dataset, compute mean_temperature and mean_magnitude for each star type. Name the result twinkle_twinkle.
🐱 This is a good place to practice focused curiosity. If you are curious about the star types, use ?stars or unique(stars$type) to understand what groups exist. Then stay focused on the main task: checking whether group_by() created one summary row for each group.

# ✅ Pre-check
data(stars)
?stars
colnames(stars)
unique(stars$type)

🗣 Add Comments: Which column is the grouping variable? Which columns are the numeric summary variables?
🎯 Write the goal: Restate the goal of this task in your own words.

twinkle_twinkle <- stars %>%

    mean_temperature = ____(_____),

twinkle_twinkle
is_grouped_df(twinkle_twinkle)

🗣 Add Comments: Does the output show one row for each star type? What does each summary column represent?

Task 2
🫒 Single grouping + three statistics
Pick one numeric fatty acid in the olive dataset, such as palmitic, oleic, or another fatty-acid variable. Group by region, then calculate:

the mean of your chosen fatty acid,
the standard deviation of your chosen fatty acid, and
the number of rows in each region.

Store the result as Olive_Garden.

# ✅ Pre-check
data(olive)
?olive
colnames(olive)
unique(olive$region)

🗣 Add Comments: Which column will you use as the grouping variable? Which fatty acid column will you summarize?
🎯 Write the goal: Restate the goal of this task in your own words.

# ⚡ Code
fatty_acid <- "_______" # You Pick!

# Pick from operators: `=`, `<-`, `%>%`, `|`, `&`, `,` `(`, and `)`
Olive_Garden <- olive ___
  group_by(region) ___
  summarize(
    mean_value = mean(.data[[fatty_acid]], na.rm = TRUE)__
    sd_value   = sd(.data[[fatty_acid]], na.rm = TRUE)__
    n          = n()__
    .groups = "drop"
  __


🧐 Notice: [[ ]] pulls one column from a data frame. If you typed olive[["oleic"]], R would use the oleic column. Here, fatty_acid stores the column name as text, so .data[[fatty_acid]] tells dplyr to use whichever column name you saved in fatty_acid.


# ✅ Check
Olive_Garden
arrange(Olive_Garden, desc(mean_value))
is_grouped_df(Olive_Garden)

🗣 Add Comments: Which region has the highest mean value for the fatty acid you selected? How many rows are in each region?

Task 3
🧮 Counting unique values
Use unique() and length() to determine how many distinct values appear in a column.
For the us_contagious_diseases dataset from dslabs, determine the number of unique diseases in the column disease.

# ✅ Pre-check

💬 Make and test a prediction
In this task, you will predict how many groups will be created when you group by both state and disease, then test your prediction with code.

Step 1
If there are 51 states in the dataset, and you assume every state has data for all 7 diseases, how many groups will group_by(state, disease) create?

categorical_counts
_____(categorical_counts)

🦠 National mean counts by disease
From us_contagious_diseases, calculate the national mean of count for each disease. Then keep only the three diseases with the highest national_mean_count. Store the result as Infectious_Burden.

title: Chapter 14: Chaining
text:
Overview
In Chapters 11, 12, and 13, we explored several functions from dplyr (select(), filter(), mutate(), case_when(), group_by and summarize()). You now know the key dplyr verbs one at a time. Lesson Overview

text:
Open your course project for RStudio
Create a new file. From the file types we have used so far, pick which file type you want to use. (File > New File > ???).
Type in the code provided in this document as you follow along with the video. Pause the video at anytime to answer assignment questions, dig deeper or add memo notes.

title: Chapter 14: Chaining
text:
🛠 Building a Pipeline
🎯 The GOAL: Find the average fuel consumption (liters/100 km) for cars in mtcars that use greater than 8 L/100 km, broken down by transmission and cylinders.

Start with the data
We’ll use the built‑in mtcars dataset.
🎯 Goal. Load mtcars and confirm shape.

data("mtcars")
# ⚡ Test:
mtcars %>%                       # rows = 32 cars, many columns
  head(2)                        # preview first two rows

head(mtcars, 2)  # base R version, same output

🗣 Data loaded correctly


Create a new variable with mutate()
We’ll calculate fuel consumption in liters per 100 kilometers (L/100 km). The formula is:
\[\frac{\text{L}}{100\text{ km}} = \frac{235.215}{\text{MPG}}\]
🎯 Goal. Add l_100km using the equation 235.215/mpg and round the value to one digit.
💬 Prediction. Higher mpg → lower l_100km (inverse).

# ⚡ Test:
mtcars %>%
  mutate(l_100km = round(235.215 / mpg, 1)) %>%
  head(2)


# ✅ Verify:
cor(mtcars$mpg, 235.215/mtcars$mpg) < 0

[1] TRUE


🗣 The inverse units are verified.


Keep only cars using greater than 8 L/100 km
We’ll only keep cars that use at least 8 L/100 km. Use filter() to keep those rows.
🎯 Goal. Keep l_100km >= 8.

# ⚡ Test:
mtcars %>%
  mutate(l_100km = round(235.215 / mpg, 1)) %>%
  filter(l_100km >= 8) %>%
  head()



Select relevant columns
🎯 Goal. Keep cyl, am, and l_100km columns.

# ⚡ Test:
mtcars2 <- mtcars %>%
  mutate(l_100km = round(235.215 / mpg, 1)) %>%
  filter(l_100km >= 8) %>%
  select(cyl, am, l_100km) %>%
  head()


# ✅ Verify:
setequal(names(mtcars2 %>% select(cyl, am, l_100km)), c("cyl","am","l_100km"))

🗣 Columns trimmed.


Group and summarize
Now we can group by am and cyl, then summarize to get the mean fuel consumption and count of cars in each group.
🎯 Goal. Mean l_100km and n by am, cyl.

# ⚡ Test:
mtcars_summary <- mtcars %>%
  mutate(l_100km = round(235.215 / mpg, 1)) %>%
  filter(l_100km >= 8) %>%
  select(cyl, am, l_100km) %>%
  group_by(am, cyl) %>%
  summarize(mean_l_100km = round(mean(l_100km), 2),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop")
mtcars_summary

🗣 Explan:
Order Matters in dplyr Pipelines. You can’t summarize groups before you define them with group_by().

group_by(am, cyl) tells dplyr to treat each unique combination of am and cyl separately. group_by() divides your data into separate groups for analysis. It doesn’t change how your data looks. It adds metadata that tells subsequent functions to operate on each group separately. It’s like telling R: “For each combination of these variables, do the following…”
summarize() then runs mean(l_100km) per group and counts rows with n().
.groups = "drop" prevents grouping in the final output.



Recode transmission for readability
❓ Question: How might you check which combination of am + cyl is least fuel‑efficient?
🎯 Goal. Label am as “Automatic/Manual” in a column “Transmission” and make it a factor with level order.

# ⚡ Test: Recode transmission for readability Method 1
mtcars_summary <- mtcars_summary %>%
  mutate(Transmission = case_when(am == 0 ~ "Automatic", TRUE ~ "Manual"),
    Transmission = factor(Transmission, levels = c("Automatic","Manual"))
  )


# ✅ Verify:
is.factor(mtcars_summary$Transmission)
identical(levels(mtcars_summary$Transmission), c("Automatic","Manual"))

🗣 Labels set; order fixed.

# ⚡ Test:✔ Pipeline complete! One readable flow from raw data to insight.
mtcars_summary <- mtcars %>%
  mutate(l_100km = round(235.215 / mpg, 1)) %>%
  filter(l_100km >= 8) %>%
  select(cyl, am, l_100km) %>%
  group_by(am, cyl) %>%
  summarize(mean_l_100km = round(mean(l_100km), 2),  
            n = n(), .groups = "drop")%>%
  mutate(am = case_when(am == 0 ~ "Automatic", TRUE ~ "Manual"),
    am = factor(am, levels = c("Automatic","Manual"))
  )
mtcars_summary

🤔 Reflect: Explain why the highest mean_l_100km is the least fuel‑efficient combination. Create a memo to earn learning skill points.


Readable Result
🎯 Goal. Build one readable pipeline, then sort by the highest Mean l/100km (higher = less efficient) and keep the top row.

mtcars_summary <- mtcars %>%
  mutate(l_100km = round(235.215 / mpg, 1)) %>%
  filter(l_100km >= 8) %>%
  select(cyl, am, l_100km) %>%
  group_by(am, cyl) %>%
  summarize(mean_l_100km = round(mean(l_100km), 2),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop")%>%
  mutate(am = case_when(am == 0 ~ "Automatic", TRUE ~ "Manual"),
    am = factor(am, levels = c("Automatic","Manual"))
  ) %>%                                       # <-- close mutate() here
  arrange(desc(mean_l_100km)) %>%             # sort highest (least efficient) first
  slice(1) %>%                                # keep the single worst combo
  rename(`Mean l/100km` = mean_l_100km,       # backticks for non-syntactic name
         Count         = n,
         Cylinder      = cyl,
         Transmission  = am)

mtcars_summary

🗣 Explain: arrange() sorts the data frame by mean_l_100km (aka Mean l/100km) in descending order, so the first row is the least fuel-efficient combination of am and cyl.
Answer the ❓ Question: Which combination of am + cyl is least fuel‑efficient?

title: Chapter 15: Probability functions
text:
Overview
Probability is easier to understand when you can build and inspect examples yourself. In this chapter, you will use R to simulate random outcomes, visualize those results, and decide whether the patterns you see are reasonable. You will work with coin flips, dice rolls, bell-shaped data, and repeated simulations so that probability feels concrete rather than abstract. These are the same kinds of tools analysts use when they need to study uncertainty, test assumptions, or estimate risk.
By the end of Chapter 15 you will be able to:
Keep these goals in mind as you move through each section.
